items.title: Eddie Palmieri — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

ctx.x: But throughout the ‘50s... I started working the Palladium in 1956 with Vicentico Valdés, who was the vocalist for Tito Puente, when my brother was in the band, and Mongo

Santamaria was the conga player. Manny Oquendo, bongo. An incredible conjunto. Conjunto meant that there was no saxes. That’s what it meant. Only Machito had an orchestra. Tito Puente was a conjunto—three trumpets and a rhythm section...timbales, conga, bongo, bass naturally, piano, and three trumpets.
We’ll talk about genres later, how charanga developed and things like that.

items.title: 52240_Frank _Machito_ Grillo oral history interview
items.q: Eddie Palmieri, all those guys. In those days I would be a millionaire.

ctx.x: No, but I mean ehhh, Marcelino Guerra, I don't - Marcelino Guerra, all of those bands, the people, they was so gungry to know what we was doing that even having that tremendous publicity that the people has now; you imagine if we would have the publicity of Willie Colon and
Eddie Palmieri, all those guys. In those days I would be a millionaire.
Uh - Huh. Okay, in 1947, in February, Stan Kenton recorded a tune called "Machito", where he paid you tribute. Do you remember that?
